reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Classic warning symptoms are sudden floaters and flashing lights (photopsia) followed by a curtain or shadow spreading across the field of vision
Central vision is preserved until the macula detaches ('macula-on' versus 'macula-off'), which is the key prognostic and timing factor
The commonest type is rhegmatogenous, caused by a retinal tear that lets fluid pass under the retina; tractional and exudative types have different mechanisms
Risk factors include high myopia, previous cataract surgery, ocular trauma, lattice degeneration, and a detachment in the fellow eye
Fundoscopy shows an elevated, mobile, often corrugated grey retina; a relative afferent pupillary defect may be present in large detachments
Treatment is surgical (laser/cryo for tears, pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, or vitrectomy) and is prioritised urgently when the macula is still attached
A posterior vitreous detachment with a fresh tear can be treated with prophylactic retinopexy to prevent progression
reference.pathophysiology: In rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a full-thickness retinal break (usually from vitreous traction as the vitreous separates with age) allows liquefied vitreous to track through the tear into the potential space between the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium, lifting the photoreceptor layer off its blood supply. Tractional detachment occurs when contracting fibrovascular membranes (as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy) pull the retina forward, and exudative detachment when fluid accumulates beneath an intact retina from inflammatory, vascular, or neoplastic processes. Separated photoreceptors become ischaemic and, if not reattached, degenerate.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation to locate breaks
Slit-lamp examination and assessment for pigment cells in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dust)
B-scan ultrasonography when the view is obscured by haemorrhage or cataract
Optical coherence tomography to determine macular status
Assessment of visual acuity and for a relative afferent pupillary defect
redFlags: Sudden new floaters and flashes with a visual field defect — sight-threatening, refer urgently
A 'macula-on' detachment is a surgical emergency because prompt repair preserves central vision
Rapidly enlarging shadow or curtain indicating extension toward the macula
New symptoms in the fellow eye of a patient with previous detachment
reference.prognosis: Anatomical reattachment is achieved in most cases with modern surgery, but final visual outcome depends heavily on whether the macula was detached and for how long before repair.
pitfalls: Dismissing floaters and flashes without a dilated peripheral retinal examination
Delaying referral in a macula-on detachment and allowing the macula to detach
Missing a small peripheral break because the retina was not examined with indentation
Attributing symptoms to migraine or vitreous floaters without excluding a tear
